title: Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience
gist: Walmart Global Tech's Aditya Mulik describes rolling a four-agent sequential LLM workflow for nightly fresh-food inventory recommendations from a 10-15 store pilot to 4,700+ US stores, the production failures that followed (vague outputs, SKU/department collisions, vanished writes, no observability) and fixes (schema + semantic validation, MCP grounding, bounded loop-agent retries, structured logging). Switching from 400 reserved PTUs to pay-as-you-go cut inference cost from ~$100-120k to ~$10k a month for the same model and tokens.

themes.theme: LLM inference cost: PTU vs pay-as-you-go

insights.claim: Walmart reserved 400 PTUs (provisioned throughput units) of a foundation model for its nightly inventory-agent workload and was charged about $100k-$120k per month.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Reserved LLM capacity is a large, visible enterprise line item; batch users are likely to churn from it.

insights.claim: Switching the same model and token volume from reserved PTUs to pay-as-you-go cut Walmart's inference bill from roughly $100k to about $10k per month, even including retries.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Batch AI workloads can see ~90% cost cuts by abandoning provisioned throughput; pressure on cloud AI reserved-capacity revenue.
insights.quote: same tokens, same model, just a pricing tier switch from PTU to pay-as-you-go

insights.claim: Reserved PTUs must be bought for 24 hours a day on monthly or yearly terms, which is wasteful for a batch job that only runs overnight and serves no live traffic.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Match inference procurement to workload shape; real-time chat justifies PTUs, overnight batch does not.

insights.claim: Pay-as-you-go brought latency and rate-limit errors, but retry logic absorbed them, and the slower nightly window did not matter because stores were closed.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Retry engineering is what makes cheaper, rate-limited tiers viable for batch AI.

insights.claim: Walmart weighed cheaper open-source models, fewer PTUs, or pay-as-you-go against foundation models such as GPT-4.1 or Gemini, framing the choice as quality versus cost, and chose to keep the foundation model on pay-as-you-go.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Enterprises are optimizing pricing tier before downgrading model quality; frontier vendors keep the workload but at lower revenue.
insights.locator: The next thing that came to us was, what AI model should I choose?

insights.claim: Walmart's existing backward-looking ML forecasts, trained on one to two years of sales history, handle steady and seasonal demand like Thanksgiving but cannot anticipate unprecedented events such as storms or competitor flash sales.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: LLM agents are being layered on top of, not replacing, classical demand forecasting at large retailers.

insights.claim: The system is a sequential four-agent workflow: a context-gathering agent (e.g., from BigQuery), a synthesis agent merging past sales data, a grounding agent adding real-time signals like weather and events, and a final agent producing a natural-language stock directive.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Reference architecture for enterprise agentic batch pipelines; drives demand for data-warehouse and MCP tooling.
insights.locator: Agents, Not Monoliths: The Sequential Workflow

insights.claim: Store managers receive a clear command such as 'increase apple stock 15%' each morning and must accept or override it, with human-in-the-loop treated as a feature rather than a fallback.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Human approval remains in the loop even at 4,700-store scale; AI value is decision support, not autonomous ordering.
insights.quote: This is a feature not a fallback.

insights.claim: The pilot on 10-15 stores produced coherent recommendations, but rolling out to all 4,700+ stores in nightly runs exposed four failures that had not appeared at small scale.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Agentic pilots systematically understate production failure rates; discount pilot-based ROI claims.
insights.quote: what works at the scale of one rarely survives the scale of thousands

insights.claim: Unstructured agent outputs gave vague high-confidence recommendations (e.g., increase 'produce items that sell well' by ~15%), fixed by schema-enforced output with typed SKU, item, department and adjustment fields.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Structured output enforcement is table stakes for enterprise LLM deployment.
insights.locator: The very first one was hallucinations and schema violations

insights.claim: Schema-valid outputs were still semantically wrong when SKU numbers collided across departments in the data ingestion layer, e.g., mapping Honeycrisp Apple to auto_parts.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Data engineering quality, not model quality, is the binding constraint on enterprise AI accuracy.
insights.quote: perfectly valid JSON, but it maps Honeycrisp Apple to auto_parts because the SKUs collided
insights.locator: Then, again, now the second failure

insights.claim: Walmart fixed semantic errors by adding an MCP tool call that validates each stock directive against the authoritative catalog data source before processing.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: MCP is being used in production as a grounding/validation layer, not just for tool access.
insights.locator: This is the part where we did the grounding mechanism

insights.claim: Network partitions and db_write timeouts silently dropped outputs, so some stores saw no recommendation and could assume nothing needed ordering.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Silent failure is a key risk of batch AI: absence of output can be misread as a positive signal.

insights.claim: Walmart replaced the sequential agent with a loop agent with bounded max-iteration retries, but warns retries must be placed where needed because unbounded retries burn tokens and cost.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Retry policy design is a direct cost lever in token-billed agent systems.
insights.quote: Retries can be a very bad loop as well

insights.claim: Observability was absent initially, leaving the team unable to tell hallucination from rate-limiting; structured logging of retries, schema violations and latency was added, targeting a 99% success rate.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Agent observability/tracing is a must-have budget item for production AI; tailwind for observability vendors.
insights.locator: Next one, so we were flying blind.

insights.claim: The initial production MVP shipped without formal evals; department-specific eval sets, grounding and governance (e.g., keeping pricing information out) were added iteratively afterward.
insights.speaker: Aditya Mulik
insights.so_what: Even large enterprises ship agentic MVPs before eval infrastructure; eval tooling demand follows deployment.
